reasons.D: Addresses the reader directly with short, dry, deflating sentences ('So is the weather.') much like the passage's 'There is no call for it' and 'but what of it?', though the wit is laid on a little more thickly.
reasons.B: Plain second-person address and short, even declaratives come close to the passage's movement, but it has little of the author's ironic undercut and closes with a hortatory instruction.
reasons.C: Keeps the direct address and some irony, but its long, balanced periods and ornate diction ('monument to the owner's want of judgment', 'diligent inspection of the premises') are more elaborate than the author's clipped plain style.
reasons.A: Uses a third-person frame ('my friend the novelist') and long, measured sentences, so it loses the confiding 'you' and the short, punchy rhythm that drive the passage.
